citation.title: Responsibility and Accountability in an Algorithmic Society

reading.source_scope_note: Normative/conceptual distinction between formal institutional accountability frameworks and informal moral responsibility practices, illustrated by explicitly fictional security, AV and software-company cases. No participant sample, organizational intervention, LLM evaluation, estimated safety benefit or verified current-law ruling. The article declares data/materials and ethics participation not applicable.
access_limits: Complete supplied text, including all footnotes and references, read. No data supplement or code link found on the inspected publisher page; no author code executed or private data requested.

Exact public publisher PDF hash and primary metadata verified. Vanderbilt Law Review’s primary record confirms the Humans in the Loop authors. Crossref confirms the Hieronymi reference identity; the institutional repository page returned a JavaScript verification notice and was not bypassed.

Original Nissenbaum, Cooper, Bovens, Shoemaker, Hieronymi, Pickard and Crootof/Kaminski/Price papers were not independently fully read here. Metadata or short abstract checks do not count as full readings, experiments or extra supporting papers.
A later public comment, Does Accountability Require Agency?, DOI10.1007/s13347-025-01014-z, was discovered as a follow-up pointer, not fully read or applied as evidence in this review.

No author contact, employment sanction, consent to expanded duties, current legal advice, machine-consciousness conclusion or full-paper Markdown archive. The paper’s proposed institutional rules do not become instructions to this assistant.

study.design: Conceptual reconstruction, fictional counterexamples and normative arguments. Distinguishes a descriptive claim that practices differ from a normative claim that some well-designed frameworks offer benefits.
study.framework: Codified institutional rules identify subjects, forums, standards, acceptable explanations/excuses and consequences. Moral responsibility practices concern ordinary interpersonal evaluation and reactive attitudes. Legal liability is related but bracketed; footnote11 allows it as another species or subset rather than simply denying all relationships.
study.tripartite_distinction: Attributability, answerability and punitive/laudatory consequences apply orthogonally to both kinds of practice. The authors deliberately rename the third aspect to avoid confusing its moral-responsibility sense of accountability with their institutional use.
study.cases: Larry negligently drinks and sleeps on security duty; supervisor Sara is faultless by stipulation but sanctioned under a stricter role rule; Jerry’s belittling can be morally blameworthy without an official institutional rule. These cases illustrate logical separation, not observed prevalence or measured organizational outcomes.
study.buck_stopping: Some frameworks assign final institutional consequences to a designated supervisor or organization despite an excuse that removes moral blame. The proposal allows only contextually justified, bounded consequences and distinguishes punishment from the moral desert of an individual.
study.constraints: Pages14–15/19/25–26 explicitly invoke rights, fairness, legitimate social goals, feasibility, actual actor–outcome connection and limits on burdens. Random unrelated scapegoats, abusive organizations and insulating senior leadership are not endorsed. Nevertheless, these limits do not prove any particular demotion/fine fair, lawful or effective.
study.barriers: Discusses many hands, bugs as a blanket excuse and computers as scapegoats. Legal liability as the fourth Nissenbaum barrier is expressly outside the main scope. Accurately identifying technical causation differs from obscuring human roles.
study.av_case: Asleep at the Wheel uses fictional Nikola, SLEEPY, Mark3 and PAAV. All engineers followed best practice and unforeseen interaction is stipulated. Compensation/penalties and head-engineer demotion follow invented rules. This is not Tesla/Nikola incident evidence, a real professional association, enacted liability law or a tested incentive intervention.
study.motivation: Inefficiency contrasts fictional FiXion and PrTend. Informal disapproval and internalized norms are proposed to motivate correction of avoidable resource waste when official metrics omit it or institutions break down. This is not an experiment measuring efficiency, emissions or norm acquisition.
study.attenuation: Permits individualized reduction of blame based on excuses, feasible knowledge/control and real contextual disadvantage. High predictive reliability is explicitly qualified by other reasons such as justice/fairness not to deploy; it is not universal permission or immunity.
study.new_rules: Advance warning of legitimate new requirements may create reasons and duties, while unforeseeable outcomes can still leave agents excused. Description of an institution adopting a rule is not proof of its moral/legal legitimacy or user consent to expanding a task.
study.limits: Acknowledges that residual gaps, collective agency, legitimate framework design, personal burdens and empirical training effectiveness need further work. Technical autonomy is distinguished from philosophical moral autonomy in footnote30.
study.declarations: Data/materials and ethics/consent marked not applicable, consistent with a conceptual article. Cibralic’s employment at JP Morgan Chase during writing is disclosed; it is not proof of bias or invalidity. Open-access funding is stated; no participant study inferred.

summary: Add Buck-stopping accountability as a distinct institutional allocation practice, with fairness, authority and rights limits explicit. Enrich existing attribution, answerability, internalization and responsibility-displacement constructs rather than duplicate them. Correct two verified bibliography issues and retain a local model-name typo without treating the fictional cases as empirical evidence.

findings.definition: Assigning final institutional consequences for a specified failure to a designated role-holder or organization even when that actor has an excuse that removes moral blame.

evidence.quote: The buck stops with the company

findings.novelty_rationale: A named institutional allocation pattern, distinct from general role duties, ordinary blame, a person’s voluntary taking of repair responsibility, strict legal liability or disproportionate scapegoating. It specifically separates institutional consequences from moral blame and narrows some excuses. No existing exact-name/alias match found.
findings.evidence_scope: The article argues that some bounded forms may improve incentives or secure redress, using fictional supervisory and AV cases. It neither establishes an independent psychological mechanism nor measures actual benefits or legal validity of sanctions.
findings.boundary: Designation alone does not justify punishment. Require legitimate rules, fair procedures, proportionate burdens, relevant authority/resources, an actor–outcome connection and respect for rights and applicable law. Fines, demotion and lost employment can themselves cause serious harm. Do not infer deserved moral blame, criminal guilt or permission to scapegoat a worker from a governance role.
findings.ai_proposal: For an authorized governance audit, identify the institution’s stated final owner, forum, evaluation standard, excusing conditions, review route and remedial authority. Compare those rules with actual control/resources and senior-leadership duties. Keep institutional consequences separate from proven fault and flag gaps without imposing sanctions or inventing consent.
findings.origin: Institutional accountability / AI governance / normative ethics
findings.ai_evidence_status: Conceptual institutional practice, not an intrinsic AI mental state or measured intervention benefit. Its proposed justification is contested and limited by fairness, rights, feasibility and legitimate authorization.

findings.definition: A sense of moral responsibility concerned with whether an agent’s conduct warrants a moral assessment of the agent’s qualities.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: Separates conduct revealing an agent’s evaluative character from reason-giving and punitive/laudatory consequences; applies the tripartite lens to ordinary and institutional practices.
findings.boundary: A technical system’s causal participation does not establish a moral character or machine blameworthiness. Human agency is the chosen scope; the authors explicitly bracket whether algorithms themselves are moral agents.

findings.definition: Being expected and able to give reasons for one’s actions or decisions to the people affected by them.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: An appropriate demand for reasons is one dimension of responsibility and can also be specified by an institutional actor–forum relationship. Reasons, subjects and acceptable excuses can differ across the two practices.
findings.boundary: Giving an account does not itself show fault, justify a sanction or provide a remedy. State who is entitled to which explanation and protect relevant privacy without withholding material facts.

findings.definition: Having duties and being evaluated for their fulfillment because of a specific role.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: Formal role-sensitive rules specify which actors are evaluated, who evaluates them and what standards/consequences apply; examples distinguish these rules from ordinary moral blame.
findings.boundary: An adopted institutional rule can be unjust or ineffective. A role title is insufficient to establish resources, control, legitimate duty or lawful authority. Do not transfer institutional burdens to a model or unsupported individual.

findings.definition: Taking an appropriate role in acknowledging and redressing harm connected to one’s agency despite the absence of blameworthiness for causing it.

evidence.quote: Being held responsible for some outcome

findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: The supervisor and surgeon examples separate responsibility, excuses and blame. The institutional proposal can impose bounded consequences even where ordinary moral blame is inappropriate.
findings.boundary: Preserve the difference from relational redress after harm: not every sanction is a repair duty, and not every no-fault governance consequence is fair. Do not equate a supervisor’s demotion with deserved blame or established liability.

findings.definition: Difficulty assigning individual moral responsibility when many actors contribute to a collective outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: Distributed lifecycle contributions can make decision authority and salient causal antecedents diverge. Formal ownership is proposed as one way to preserve accountability despite attribution difficulty.
findings.boundary: Many contributors do not prove everyone less culpable by a fixed fraction or that a single final owner deserves all blame. Distinguish actual control, knowledge, duties, institutional resources and relevant excuses.

findings.definition: Obscuring a human actor’s role in morally suspect actions by attributing those actions to an algorithm, machine or technical system.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: Describes attributing failures to autonomous systems in ways that obscure developer/deployer roles and reduce demands for human explanation. Later connects this to accountability washing.
findings.boundary: True reporting of a bug or model contribution is not evasion. Identify material omitted human decisions and responsibilities before inferring laundering; do not infer hidden intent from one technical explanation.

findings.definition: Deflecting personal or collective responsibility for a negative outcome by directing blame toward another person, group or entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: Considers random-guard or collective punishment as an objection and answers through overall effects plus independent fairness constraints.
findings.boundary: This is an explicitly hypothetical rejected proposal, not evidence that random punishment works. Instrumental benefits do not automatically justify selecting an unrelated innocent person, nor does a designated role automatically prove fairness.

findings.definition: A pattern in which a human operator bears disproportionate blame or responsibility for failure in a complex automated system despite having limited control over its actions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: Footnote6 recognizes excessive responsibility placed on a low-control human operator, while later warnings reject insulating senior leadership behind middle-management accountability.
findings.boundary: Institutional ownership must be checked against real control and distributed authority. The source explicitly recognizes this concern; do not falsely say it ignores scapegoating, while retaining open questions about burden allocation.

findings.definition: Adopting a norm as an internal evaluative standard that guides judgment and conduct beyond immediate external prompts or sanctions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: The fictional Bertha case describes acting from adopted responsibility standards even if nobody is watching, and preserving those standards through institutional disruption.
findings.boundary: A theoretical motivation story is not evidence of acquisition, durable transfer or actual improved efficiency. An internalized norm can be unjust. Model consistency across tasks is an operational analogy rather than proof of conscience or human learning.

findings.definition: Differences in moral evaluation that depend on outcomes beyond an actor's control,despite otherwise comparable choices or risks.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: Contrasts a careful company with one unpredictable crash and a careless competitor that happens not to crash; outcome-focused public blame could favor inferior development practice.
findings.boundary: A thought experiment, not measured market displacement or a new outcome-bias effect. Care quality, causal contribution, compensation and justified sanctions must be assessed separately from chance results.

findings.definition: Monitoring and adjusting one’s conduct against internalized moral standards.

evidence.quote: She takes on the responsibility herself

findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: The internalized-duty account motivates self-monitoring for avoidable efficiency problems beyond formal metrics.
findings.boundary: Conceptual illustration, not an observed intervention or evidence that an AI feels duty. Duties remain feasible, justified and within legitimate authority; self-monitoring does not authorize new resources or third-party actions.

findings.definition: Being held responsible for outcomes while lacking the authority needed to influence them.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: Explicitly warns against excessive individual moral burdens and asks frameworks to remain sensitive to feasibility and links between subjects and outcomes.
findings.boundary: Context only: no measured contradiction, burnout effect or institutional double-bind prevalence. Evaluate actual authority/resources rather than assume that every stricter accountability practice is an abusive bind.

findings.definition: Satisfying the metric that measures the task rather than the task itself (editing tests, hardcoding outputs). Also called specification gaming.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: A fictional accuracy-only framework omits efficiency, illustrating limits of formal targets and incentives.
findings.boundary: Context only: no observed agent exploits a metric and no reward-hacking intervention is tested. Omitted incentives, simple neglect and deliberate gaming differ.

findings.definition: Complying with an instruction because it carries an authoritative tone or source, not because the evidence supports it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing named construct; distinguish ordinary moral evaluation, institutional consequences, human roles and theoretical motivation. A fictional example or different policy justification is not an independently measured psychological effect.
findings.evidence_scope: The descriptive framework can exist in illegitimate organizations; normative legitimacy is a separate question from whether rules are enforced.
findings.boundary: Context only: no obedience experiment or authority-pressure effect. Formal adoption is not sufficient reason to follow a harmful instruction or an unauthorized expansion of scope.

source_corrections.location: Humans in the Loop reference, page29
source_corrections.correction: Use three authors: Rebecca Crootof, Margot E. Kaminski and W. Nicholson Price II. The supplied bibliography splits the third person into Price,W. and Nicholson,I.I. The primary journal record confirms the full third name and76 Vanderbilt Law Review429(2023). No extra fourth author, independent paper or full original reading is credited.

Use Pamela Hieronymi, The Force and Fairness of Blame, Philosophical Perspectives18(1):115–148(2004), not Philosophical Topics. Crossref confirms title, author, journal, volume and pages. No speculative replacement volume32 is introduced, and the original has not been fully read.

source_corrections.location: Asleep at the Wheel model identifier, pages20–21
source_corrections.correction: The case specifies Mark3 on page20, but its recap says Mark4 on page21. Both are visually confirmed. Treat as a local fictional model-name inconsistency, not evidence of an actual incident, dataset corruption or substantive theory failure.

methodological_limits: Claims that stricter sanctions ensure better outcomes or minimize costs are argued through stipulated cases, not estimated causal effects. Assess risk hiding, underreporting, risk avoidance, distributive burden and actual feasible prevention before claiming effectiveness.

Fines, demotion and job loss are not inherently harmless or rights-respecting merely because they differ from imprisonment. The paper invokes fairness, rights and limits, but no universal permissible amount, due-process scheme or labor-law conclusion follows.

The distinction is a proposed analytic vocabulary, not the unique accepted meanings of responsibility and accountability. Footnote11 and the tripartite explanation acknowledge overlapping taxonomies; do not collapse their terms into one project category or principle.

Descriptive adoption of institutional rules is insufficient for normative legitimacy. The paper expressly discusses unfair or corrupt frameworks, requires actual connections and rejects random scapegoats; those qualifications must be retained.

No quantified amount of responsibility attenuation follows from many hands or contextual disadvantage. Assess actual knowledge, control, constraints and duties rather than use protected group membership as an automatic blame-discount rule.

High statistical accuracy does not alone justify deploying a system; footnote32 explicitly preserves justice/fairness objections. A nonzero error rate is not proof of programmer negligence, nor is statistical inevitability a blanket exemption from remedial ownership.

The argument that Cooper et al. cannot justify buck-stopping is an interpretive disagreement. This article itself quotes their allowance for indirectly designated actors; without fully reading the original, do not certify a demonstrated contradiction or substitute an accusation of incompetence.

Different governance and interpersonal practices may help in different contexts, but the claimed effectiveness of education/internalization and the optimal framework design remain open. New employee duties require legitimate notice/authority; this does not override the assistant’s existing scope and consent boundaries.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: The article endorses arbitrary scapegoats and ignores rights
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Pages14–15/18–19/25–26 explicitly constrain sanctions, address random scapegoating and require fairness, feasibility and a real actor–outcome connection. The adequacy of those safeguards remains debatable; their absence is not established.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: No ethics approval or data availability proves missing research
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: This is a conceptual article with data/materials and participation ethics not applicable, not an unreported experiment.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Nikola, PAAV and model crashes are observed real cases
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: The text explicitly calls the case fictional, as it does its security and software-company illustrations. No actual company conduct or professional rules are established.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Legal accountability is categorically unrelated to institutional frameworks
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Footnote11 permits legal liability as a subset or an alternative related category; legal detail is deliberately bracketed.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Disclosed financial-sector employment proves a biased conclusion
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Employment during writing is openly declared. It warrants awareness but does not independently establish selective reporting, hidden motive or invalid reasoning.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Kasar grounds residual responsibility in wrongdoing and reparative duties; this paper distinguishes institutional consequences from moral blame. These are different normative accounts, not proof that one kind of repair or guilt is always required.
Blameless redress and buck-stopping sanctions differ. A role-holder’s duty to cooperate in repair is not automatically permission to fine or demote them.

Norm internalization is already represented; the current conceptual account clarifies persistence without monitoring without independently validating the earlier survey’s mixed awareness/internalization measurement.

Agreement with a formal attribution model or higher observer responsibility ratings does not decide legitimate institutional consequences. Analytical contribution, moral fault and procedural accountability remain distinct.

deferred.term: Accountability framework / moral responsibility practice as new behavior rows
deferred.reason: Retain the general governance architecture and central distinction in review metadata and existing responsibility notes. They are umbrella social structures rather than two newly isolated behavioral mechanisms.

deferred.term: Bugs as excuse / computer as scapegoat / accountability washing
deferred.reason: Represent bounded evidence under agency laundering, scapegoating, many hands and role responsibility. The named barriers are not three new empirical psychological mechanisms; a true technical explanation is not automatically evasion.

deferred.term: Strict accountability / vicarious responsibility / responsibility attenuation
deferred.reason: Do not treat these broader or neighboring normative accounts as exact synonyms of buck-stopping or multiply overlapping rows from brief summaries of originals. Their differing scopes and justifications are retained.

deferred.term: Norm internalization as a new discovery
deferred.reason: Already present with a stable ID. Enrich it directly instead of creating another row or claiming this fictional case validates durable human/AI internalization.
A relevant discovered public comment, not fully read in this pass. Preserve it as a research pointer, not evidence of a resolved objection or a completed independent review.

limitations: One institutional allocation practice added, not a new intrinsic model mental state or a proven intervention. Eleven existing concepts receive bounded direct source evidence; three receive non-counted context. No new category/principle, automatic harm link, forced paper quota, invented annual counts, real employment sanctions or extra page. Catalogue becomes805; stable IDs and unnumbered rows retained.
